translation: Sundarlal was just preparing to go to Amritsar border when he received news of Lajo's arrival. Sundarlal was immediately flustered by such news. His foot immediately moved towards the door, but he turned back. He wanted to get angry and sit down spreading all the committee's placards and flags, and then cry. But there, such a display of emotions was not possible. He manly faced this inner struggle and, measuring his steps, walked towards Chowki Kalan, because that was the place where the abducted women were delivered. Now Lajo stood before him, trembling with a feeling of fear. Only she knew Sundarlal. No one else knew. He used to treat her like that even before, and now that she had come after spending days of her life with another man, who knows what he would do. Sundarlal looked at Lajo. She was wearing a purely Islamic-style red dupatta and had her veil drawn on the left side. It was merely out of habit, a habit of blending in with other women and ultimately having the ease of escaping her captor's snare. And she was thinking so much about Sunderlal that she didn't even think of changing her clothes or adjusting her dupatta properly. She was unable to distinguish between the fundamental differences of Hindu and Muslim culture, between a right-side veil and a left-side veil. Now she stood before Sunderlal, trembling with a feeling of both hope and fear. Sunderlal felt a jolt. He saw that Lajwanti's complexion had brightened somewhat, and she looked a bit healthier than before. No, she had gotten fat. Everything Sunderlal had imagined about Lajo was wrong. He thought that after dissolving in sorrow, Lajwanti would have become completely emaciated, and her voice would not come out of her mouth. He was greatly shocked by the thought that she had been very happy in Pakistan, but he remained silent because he had sworn to remain silent. Although he couldn't understand that if she was so happy, then why did she come back? He thought that perhaps due to the pressure of the Indian government, she had to come here against her will. But there was one thing he couldn't understand: Lajwanti's darkened face was tinged with yellowness, and due to sheer sorrow, the flesh of her body had left her bones. She had become fat from an excess of sorrow and appeared healthy. But this was such a health that after walking two steps, a person would lose their breath. Upon casting the first glance at Mughviya's face, the impression was somewhat strange, but he confronted all thoughts with a resolute manliness. Many other people were also present. Someone said, "We do not take the leavings of a Muslim woman." And this voice was lost in the slogans of Rasalu, Nekiram, and the old clerk of Chauki Kalan. Separate from all these voices, Kalka Prasad's cracking and shouting voice was coming. He would cough and also keep speaking. He had become intensely convinced of this new reality, this new purification. It seemed as if today he had read some new Veda, some new Purana, and some new Shastra, and in this achievement of his, he wanted to make others partners too. Surrounded by all these people and their voices, Lajo and Sundarlal were going to their dwelling. And it seemed as if Ramchandra and Sita of thousands of years ago were returning to Ayodhya after a very long moral exile. On one hand, people were celebrating with rows of lamps in expression of joy, and on the other hand, there was regret over them being subjected to such a long torment. Even after Lajwanti's departure, Sundarlal Babu had continued the 'Basaao' program with the same intensity. He had fulfilled it both in word and deed. And those people who saw only empty sentimentality in Sundarlal's words began to be convinced. Often, there was happiness in people's hearts, and mostly, there was regret in their hearts. Besides the widow of the house, many women from Mullah Shakur's neighborhood were hesitant to come to Social Worker Sunderlal's house. But Sunderlal didn't care about anyone's attention or inattention. The queen of his heart had arrived, and the lotus of his heart had bloomed. Sunderlal had enshrined Lajo's golden idol in the temple of his heart, and he himself sat at the door, guarding it. Lajo, who used to remain timid with fear, slowly began to open up after seeing Sunderlal's unexpected gentle behavior. Sunderlal no longer called Lajwanti by the name Lajo. He called her "Devi," and Lajo would go mad with an unknown joy. How much she wanted to tell Sunderlal her story and cry so much while telling it that all her sins would be washed away. But Sunderlal avoided listening to Lajo's stories, and Lajo, even in her openness, remained somewhat withdrawn.
